stops.name: Cairo, physician to Saladin
stops.campa: By the year of Saladin's full mastery of Egypt and Syria, Moses attends the sultan himself, called upon for the great man's health as for that of his household, though never, so far as the record shows, granted the intimacy of a true court favorite; he remains a subject physician summoned as needed, not a courtier by rank. It is a strange point on the map for a rabbi of Córdoba to reach: physician to the very general whose armies will retake Jerusalem from the Crusader kingdom Moses himself passed through as a refugee pilgrim, twenty years before.

stops.name: Fustat, the birth of Abraham
stops.campa: Late in life, after years without an heir to carry forward the line his father's flight from Córdoba was meant to preserve, a son is born to Moses: Abraham, who will grow to succeed him in nearly every office, Nagid, court physician, head of the yeshiva, and defend and extend his father's teaching against its critics for forty years after this. The Maimonides name, which very nearly ended with a shipwrecked merchant and a dead judge in two countries of exile, will run in the office of Nagid for four generations more through this single surviving child.

stops.name: Jerusalem falls to Saladin, the circle closed
stops.campa: On the second of October Saladin's army enters Jerusalem, and the Frankish kingdom that once let a refugee rabbi from Fez climb the Haram and pray on the Temple platform is finished after eighty-eight years. Moses is fifty and physician to the household of the conqueror. The city he prayed in as a stateless pilgrim, keeping the sixth of Marcheshvan ever after as a private festival, now belongs to the sultan whose pulse he takes. Saladin opens the city to Jewish resettlement, and Jews return to live in Jerusalem for the first time since the Crusaders killed or expelled them in 1099.

stops.name: Cairo, the Regimen of Health for al-Afdal
stops.campa: At the request of al-Malik al-Afdal, Saladin's eldest son and briefly ruler after him, Moses composes the Regimen of Health, a consilium in Arabic on diet, exercise, sleep, and the moderation of the passions, grounded in Galen but bent toward practical counsel for a prince whose excesses have made him ill. It is medicine as the Guide for the Perplexed is theology: Greek science reasoned through to a rule of living any careful man, prince or pauper, Muslim or Jew, might actually follow. Ten such treatises will eventually carry his name into the medical schools of Latin Europe under the name Rabbi Moyses.

stops.name: Fustat, the letter on the impossible day
stops.campa: To Samuel ibn Tibbon, his Provençal translator, eager to cross the sea and question him face to face about the Guide, Moses writes back a description of a day that makes the visit impossible: up before dawn to attend the sultan in Cairo, not home again until afternoon, faint with hunger, and then the anteroom of his own house filled with patients, Jews and Gentiles both, physicians and commoners, until two hours or more into the night, so that he can barely speak from exhaustion by the time the last has gone. He asks Ibn Tibbon to put his questions in writing instead.
stops.quote: I dwell at Fostat, and the sultan resides at Cairo... My duties to the sultan are very heavy. I am obliged to visit him every day, early in the morning... I do not return to Fostat until the afternoon. Then I am almost dying with hunger... Patients go in and out until nightfall, and sometimes even, I solemnly assure you, until two hours or more in the night.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, c. 1199

stops.name: Fustat, the Guide for the Perplexed begun
stops.campa: For his most gifted student, Joseph ben Judah of Ceuta, who has studied with him and gone on still hungry for the harder questions no code of law can settle, the tension between the Torah's plain word and the philosophy of Aristotle, the nature of prophecy, the limits of what can be said of God at all, Moses begins a work in Judeo-Arabic addressed to him directly: Dalalat al-Ha'irin, Guide of the Perplexed. He writes it deliberately scattered on the surface, its true argument assembled only by a reader already trained in both Torah and philosophy at once.
stops.quote: Your absence moved me to compose this Treatise, which I have composed for you and for those like you, however few they are.
stops.quote_source: Guide for the Perplexed, Dedicatory Epistle to Joseph ben Judah

stops.name: Fustat, the Guide completed
stops.campa: The Guide stands finished: three books moving from the true meaning of Scripture's anthropomorphic language, God has no body, no attributes, is known only by negation, through a cosmology borrowed from Aristotle and the Arab commentators, to a final account of providence, prophecy, and the reasons behind the commandments that reads the whole of Jewish law as a school for intellect and will together. It reconciles, for a reader able to follow it, the philosopher's God of pure necessary being with the Torah's God who speaks to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, and unsettles, for readers unable to follow it, every comfortable literalism they had brought to the text.

stops.name: Fustat, answering the doubters of resurrection
stops.campa: Word reaches Fustat that some readers, in Yemen and closer to home, take the Guide's insistence on an incorporeal World to Come as a denial of the bodily resurrection of the dead, one of his own thirteen principles set down twenty years before. Moses answers with the Treatise on Resurrection, affirming the doctrine plainly as a matter of tradition and revelation even while holding to his philosophical account of the soul's ultimate, bodiless felicity. It is the last great controversy of his lifetime, proof that a mind trusted with the whole of the law and the whole of Aristotle at once will still be read, by some, as having betrayed one for the other.

stops.name: Fustat, death
stops.campa: Moses ben Maimon dies in Fustat at the end of a life that carried him from a judge's house in Córdoba through the disguise of Fez, the harbor of Acre, the ruined Temple platform and the patriarchs' cave, to the citadel of two sultans and the desk from which the whole law of Israel was rewritten in fourteen books. Word of his death brings public mourning across Fustat and Cairo alike, Jew and Muslim, for a physician whose hand had touched half the city and a Nagid whose rulings had touched every Jewish house in Egypt. His son Abraham, eighteen years old, inherits every office at once.

stops.name: The road to Tiberias, the body's last journey
stops.campa: Tradition holds that Moses had asked to be buried in the Land of Israel, and that his body is carried north out of Egypt along the coastal road his own family had fled down in the other direction, thirty-nine years before. The legend his students tell afterward has the camel choosing its own resting place: walking without a driver's hand until it stops, unbidden, beside the grave of Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai at Tiberias, sage of the generation after the Temple's fall, as though the dead were seeking their own company across a thousand years.

stops.name: Tiberias, the tomb and the pilgrimage of the Twentieth of Tevet
stops.campa: He is laid to rest beside the Sea of Galilee, in Tiberias, one of Judaism's four holy cities, under a tomb that will be visited, argued over, rebuilt, and covered in time with fourteen inscribed columns, seven to a side, one for each book of the Mishneh Torah, an epitaph in architecture for the work he considered his own truest monument. The community fixes his death-day, the twentieth of Tevet, as an annual pilgrimage, against, tradition admits, his own express teaching that a Jew owes no cultic reverence to any grave. They come anyway, every year, in numbers that only grow.
stops.quote: From Moses to Moses arose none like Moses.
stops.quote_source: Traditional epitaph inscribed at the Tomb of Maimonides, Tiberias
